L50@P1-2: Have your say 71 This is a booklet about heart rhythms. It includes
L51@P2: information on both normal and abnormal
L52@P2: heart rhythms.
L53@P2: An abnormal heart rhythm is called an arrhythmia
L54@P2: (pronounced ‘ah-rith-me-ah’).
L55@P2: Some people who have an arrhythmia may feel
L56@P2: unwell, and being diagnosed with an arrhythmia
L57@P2: can cause some anxiety, even if your condition is
L58@P2: not harmful. Getting appropriate information and
L59@P2: support can be very helpful, and can help improve
L60@P2: your quality of life.
L61@P2: This booklet explains:
L62@P2: • what a normal heart rhythm is
L63@P2: • what palpitations are
L64@P2: • what ectopic beats are (when you feel like your
L65@P2: heart ‘misses’ a beat or you feel extra beats)
L66@P2: • the different types of arrhythmias – what they
L67@P2: are and what causes them
L68@P2: ABOUT THIS BOOKLET 03
L69@P2: • the tests used to diagnose arrhythmias, and
L70@P2: • the treatments you might need to have if you
L71@P2: have an arrhythmia.
L72@P2: This booklet does not replace the advice that the
L73@P2: health professionals involved in your care may
L74@P2: give you, but it should help you to understand
L75@P2: what they tell you.
L76@P2: If you have atrial fibrillation
L77@P2: Atrial fibrillation is the most common type of
L78@P2: arrhythmia. We mention it in this booklet but,
L79@P2: if you have atrial fibrillation, you will find more
L80@P2-3: information in our booklet Atrial fibrillation (AF). WHAT IS AN ARRHYTHMIA?
L81@P3: An arrhythmia is an abnormal heart rhythm. Your
L82@P3: heart has an electrical conduction system which
L83@P3: makes your heart pump blood around your body.
L84@P3: Arrhythmias are caused by an abnormality in that
L85@P3: electrical conduction system, and can make your
L86@P3: heart beat too slowly, too quickly, or in an irregular
L87@P3: way. Some arrhythmias are more serious than others.
L88@P3: There are many reasons why someone may develop
L89@P3: an arrhythmia. For example, they are more common
L90@P3: in older people, and in people with a heart condition
L91@P3: such as coronary heart disease, an enlarged heart, or
L92@P3: heart valve disease.
L93@P3: The symptoms of an arrhythmia will depend on what
L94@P3: type of arrhythmia you have, and how it affects the
L95@P3: way your heart works. The most common symptoms
L96@P3: of an arrhythmia include palpitations (which might
L97@P3: feel like a thumping or fluttering sensation in your
L98@P3: chest), dizziness, breathlessness, and in some cases
L99@P3: collapsing or losing consciousness.
L100@P3: There are many different types of arrhythmias.
L101@P3: This booklet describes the most common types.
L102@P3: HOW A NORMAL HEART WORKS
L103@P3: Your heart is a muscular pump which pumps blood
L104@P3: through to your lungs, your brain, and the rest of
L105@P3: your body. It has four chambers – two upper ones
L106@P3: called the right and left atria, and two lower ones
L107@P3: called the right and left ventricles. See the diagram
L108@P3: on the next page.
L109@P3: Your heart’s pumping action is controlled by tiny
L110@P3: electrical impulses produced by a part of the right
L111@P3: atrium called the sinus node. The sinus node is
L112@P3: sometimes called your heart’s ‘natural pacemaker’.
L113@P3: These impulses make the atria contract and push
L114@P3: blood into the ventricles. The impulses travel to the
L115@P3: ventricles through the AV node (atrio-ventricular
L116@P3: node). This acts like a junction box and is sometimes
L117@P3: called the AV junction. When the impulse reaches the
L118@P3: ventricles, the ventricles both contract, pushing the
L119@P3: blood out of your heart to your lungs, your brain, and
L120@P3: the rest of your body. In a normal heart rhythm, each
L121@P3: impulse from the sinus node makes the atria and the
L122@P3: ventricles contract regularly.
L123@P3-4: 05Normal electrical signals in the heart
L124@P4: left atrium
L125@P4: AV node
L126@P4: left ventricle
L127@P4: sinus node
L128@P4: electrical
L129@P4: impulses
L130@P4: coming
L131@P4: from the
L132@P4: sinus node

L135@P4: While you are resting, your sinus node normally
L136@P4: produces between 60 and 100 impulses a minute.
L137@P4: It’s your heart pumping the blood that produces
L138@P4: your pulse, which you can feel, for example, at the
L139@P4: artery in your wrist. The rate and rhythm of your
L140@P4: heart can be measured by taking your pulse.
L141@P4: The rate is how quickly your heart beats, and the
L142@P4: rhythm is how regular or irregular the beats are.
L143@P4-5: 07How to measure your heart rate by taking
L144@P5: your pulse
L145@P5: Every heartbeat creates a wave of pressure, as blood
L146@P5: flows along the arteries. Where these arteries lie
L147@P5: closest to the surface of your skin, you can feel this
L148@P5: pressure wave as a pulse.
L149@P5: 08 CHECKING YOUR PULSE
L150@P5: To measure your pulse, you’ll need a clock or
L151@P5: watch that measures seconds.
L152@P5: 1 Hold one of your hands out so you’re looking
L153@P5: at your palm.
L154@P5: 2 Place the pads of the first and middle fingers
L155@P5: of your other hand on the inside of your wrist.
L156@P5: You should place them at the base of your
L157@P5: thumb, near where a watch strap would sit.
L158@P5: 3 Press lightly and feel the pulse. If you can’t feel
L159@P5: anything, press slightly harder or move your
L160@P5: fingers around until you feel your pulse.
L161@P5: 4 Once you’ve found your pulse, count how many
L162@P5: beats you can feel during 60 seconds.
L163@P5: A normal heart rate is between 60 and 100 beats per
L164@P5: minute while you are resting.
L165@P5: You can also feel the rhythm of your pulse and check
L166@P5-6: if it’s regular or irregular.What to do if your pulse is irregular
L167@P6: An irregular pulse could be a sign that you have an
L168@P6: arrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation (AF). AF is a major
L169@P6: cause of stroke, so it’s important to find out if you have
L170@P6: it. If you think you have an irregular pulse, or if you‘re
L171@P6: concerned about your pulse, make an appointment
L172@P6: to see your doctor.
L173@P6: 10 NORMAL HEART RHYTHMS
L174@P6: The heart’s normal rhythm is called sinus rhythm.
L175@P6: Its rate is between 60 and 100 beats per minute (bpm)
L176@P6: while you are resting.
L177@P6: If the sinus rhythm is slower than 60 bpm, it’s called
L178@P6: sinus bradycardia. If the sinus rhythm is faster than
L179@P6: 100 bpm, it’s called sinus tachycardia.
L180@P6: The normal heart rate varies from minute to minute,
L181@P6: depending on the demands on the heart. Sinus
L182@P6: arrhythmia is a normal variation of sinus rhythm,
L183@P6: where the heart rate increases very slightly as you
L184@P6: take a breath in.
L185@P6: Sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia
L186@P6: and sinus arrhythmia are all normal heart rhythms
L187@P6: where the electrical impulses travel in a normal way
L188@P6: through the heart.
L189@P6-7: 11Sinus bradycardia
L190@P7: Many people get sinus bradycardia (a slow heart
L191@P7: rate), especially when they are resting or asleep.
L192@P7: People who are very physically active are more
L193@P7: likely to have slower heart rates.
L194@P7: Other causes of sinus bradycardia include:
L195@P7: • medicines such as beta-blockers, including eye
L196@P7: drops which contain beta-blockers
L197@P7: • an underactive thyroid gland
L198@P7: • hypothermia, and
L199@P7: • tachybrady syndrome (see page 50).
L200@P7: Treatment
L201@P7: Sinus bradycardia does not usually need treatment.
L202@P7: However, if your sinus bradycardia is due to an
L203@P7: underlying condition – such as an underactive
L204@P7: thyroid gland – you may need to have treatment
L205@P7: for that condition.
L206@P7: 12
L207@P7: Sinus tachycardia
L208@P7: Your heart may be beating fast because it needs to –
L209@P7: for example, if you’re doing exercise, or if you’re
L210@P7: excited. It can also beat faster if you’re stressed or
L211@P7: anxious, or in pain.
L212@P7: Sometimes a sinus tachycardia is a sign of an
L213@P7: underlying condition such as an overactive thyroid
L214@P7: gland (thyrotoxicosis) or severe anaemia. Or it may
L215@P7: be because you are dehydrated, or have an infection
L216@P7: or have had severe blood loss.
L217@P7: Other causes of sinus tachycardia include:
L218@P7: • stimulants such as caffeine, nicotine and alcohol
L219@P7: • prescribed medicines such as salbutamol
L220@P7: (Ventolin) – a medicine for asthma, or
L221@P7: • illegal drugs such as amphetamines (speed),
L222@P7: cocaine, ecstasy and cannabis.
L223@P7: Treatment
L224@P7: Treatment is rarely needed. However, if an underlying
L225@P7: condition is causing the sinus tachycardia, you may
L226@P7: need to have treatment.
L227@P7-8: 13PALPITATIONS
L228@P8: The term ‘palpitations’ is often used to describe the
L229@P8: sensation of feeling your own heart beating. Some
L230@P8: people say palpitations feel like:
L231@P8: • a fluttering in their chest, or
L232@P8: • their heart pounding, or
L233@P8: • a thud or movement in their chest.
L234@P8: Some say they feel their palpitations in their neck or
L235@P8: through their ear when they are lying down.
L236@P8: Most people who get palpitations don’t have a serious
L237@P8: heart condition, but palpitations can feel unpleasant
L238@P8: and may cause distress. They are common, and many
L239@P8: people will have them at some time in their lives.
L240@P8: If you’re concerned about palpitations, make an
L241@P8: appointment to see your doctor. They may arrange for
L242@P8: you to have an ECG. You may also need a 24-hour ECG
L243@P8: recording. We describe these tests on page 19.
L244@P8: Palpitations are common,
L245@P8: and many people will
L246@P8: have them at some time
L247@P8-9: in their lives. ECTOPIC BEATS
L248@P9: Ectopic beats are early (premature) or extra
L249@P9: heartbeats that can cause palpitations, and can
L250@P9: make you feel like your heart skips or misses a beat.
L251@P9: An ectopic beat happens when cells other than the
L252@P9: sinus node release an electrical discharge, causing an
L253@P9: ‘extra’ or early heartbeat. There is often a pause after
L254@P9: the extra beat, giving the sensation of a ‘missed’ beat.
L255@P9: Ectopic beats can happen in patterns – for example,
L256@P9: there may be one before every other normal
L257@P9: heartbeat, or three ectopic beats in a row.
L258@P9: Most people have ectopic beats at some time in their
L259@P9: lives, and most are unaware of having them, or may
L260@P9: have them while asleep. Some people have them
L261@P9: often, but don’t have any symptoms, while others
L262@P9: may have very few but have symptoms such as
L263@P9: palpitations.
L264@P9: Most people who get ectopic beats have nothing to
L265@P9: worry about. People of all ages can get them, and in
L266@P9: most cases the ectopic beats are not caused by an
L267@P9: underlying heart condition, are not dangerous and
L268@P9: don’t need treatment.
L269@P9: Ectopic beats can be confirmed by an ECG or by a
L270@P9: 24-hour ECG recording. If ectopic beats are seen on
L271@P9: your ECG and you have an underlying heart condition,
L272@P9: you may need to have some more tests (see page 19).
L273@P9: If you have no underlying heart condition, and
L274@P9: your doctor tells you that the ectopic beats are
L275@P9: harmless, it’s unlikely you’ll need to have any more
L276@P9: tests or treatment.
L277@P9-10: 17ARRHYTHMIAS (ABNORMAL HEART RHYTHMS)
L278@P10: What are the symptoms of an arrhythmia?
L279@P10: Symptoms can include palpitations (see page 14),
L280@P10: dizziness, breathlessness, and in some cases,
L281@P10: collapsing or becoming unconscious.
L282@P10: What types of arrhythmia are there?
L283@P10: There are many different types of arrhythmia. What
L284@P10: type you have will depend on where in your heart
L285@P10: the rhythm starts, and whether it causes your heart
L286@P10: to beat too fast, or too slow.
L287@P10: We describe the most common types of arrhythmias
L288@P10: on pages 26 to 51. These include:
L289@P10: • fast heart rhythms – called tachycardias, and
L290@P10: • heart blocks and slow heart rhythms – called
L291@P10: bradycardias.
L292@P10: Tests and treatment
L293@P10: On the next page we describe the different tests that
L294@P10: are used to diagnose arrhythmias. On pages 36 and 52
L295@P10: we explain the treatments you might have if you are
L296@P10: diagnosed with an arrhythmia.
L297@P10: TESTS TO DIAGNOSE ARRHYTHMIAS 19
L298@P10: Below we describe some of the tests used to diagnose
L299@P10: different types of arrhythmias. For more detailed
L300@P10: information, see our booklet Tests.
L301@P10: ECG
L302@P10: This is also called an electrocardiogram.
L303@P10: An ECG records the electrical activity of your heart.
L304@P10: It can show an arrhythmia, but only if it is happening
L305@P10: at the time of the ECG. Sometimes an ECG can
L306@P10: show features that suggest you might be at risk
L307@P10: of an arrhythmia.
L308@P10: An ECG is painless and usually takes about five
L309@P10: minutes to do. Small sticky patches called ‘electrodes’
L310@P10: are put on your chest, arms and legs and are
L311@P10: connected, by wires, to a recording machine.
L312@P10: The recording machine picks up the electrical activity
L313@P10: in your heart and interprets it into wavy lines which
L314@P10: are printed onto paper.
L315@P10: If your ECG shows an abnormal heart rhythm, it’s a
L316@P10: good idea for your doctor to give you a copy of the
L317@P10: ECG, as well as keeping a copy in your medical records.
L318@P10: If you ever go to an emergency department with an
L319@P10-11: arrhythmia, take the copy of your ECG with you. 24-hour ECG recording
L320@P11: This is also called Holter monitoring or ambulatory
L321@P11: ECG monitoring.
L322@P11: This can be useful if a standard ECG doesn’t pick up
L323@P11: an arrhythmia but you are getting symptoms quite
L324@P11: often. You have to wear a small recording machine,
L325@P11: usually around your waist. Four or six ECG leads from
L326@P11: the device are taped to your chest. The device records
L327@P11: an ECG over a 24-hour period – through one day and
L328@P11: overnight. Sometimes the recorder can record for
L329@P11: longer than 24 hours.
L330@P11: Exercise ECG
L331@P11: This is also called an exercise tolerance test or ETT.
L332@P11: This is an ECG recording that is taken while you
L333@P11: are walking on a treadmill or while cycling on an
L334@P11: exercise bike.
L335@P11: Sometimes underlying heart conditions can cause
L336@P11: arrhythmias. An exercise ECG monitors your heart
L337@P11: while you’re exercising and when your heart is
L338@P11: working under increased pressure.
L339@P11: 20 21
L340@P11: Cardiac event recorders
L341@P11: If you have symptoms that don’t happen frequently,
L342@P11: you may be given a small electrical recording device
L343@P11: to keep with you, so you can record your heart’s rate
L344@P11: and rhythm at particular times. The hospital staff will
L345@P11: tell you how to record any irregular rhythm that you
L346@P11: feel, and how to send the recording to them.
L347@P11: Cardiac memory device
L348@P11: A cardiac memory device is a type of cardiac event
L349@P11: recorder. When you feel an irregular heart rhythm,
L350@P11: you hold the device to your chest to make a recording.
L351@P11: You then transmit the recording to your hospital
L352@P11: by placing the device next to the mouthpiece of
L353@P11: your phone.
L354@P11: Implantable loop recorder
L355@P11: An implantable loop recorder is a small, slim device
L356@P11: – about the size of a packet of chewing gum or a
L357@P11: computer memory stick – which is implanted under
L358@P11: the skin. (Some newer devices are even smaller than
L359@P11: this.) You activate the device when you feel the
L360@P11: abnormal rhythm. The hospital staff will show you
L361@P11-12: how to do this.Electrophysiological studies
L362@P12: This is also called an EP study, EPS or
L363@P12: electrophysiological testing.
L364@P12: An EP study aims to discover if there are extra
L365@P12: electrical pathways in the heart that could be causing
L366@P12: an abnormal heart rhythm – especially a particular
L367@P12: type of fast heart rhythm called an SVT (see page 26).
L368@P12: If you need an EP study, your doctor will refer you to
L369@P12: a cardiac electrophysiologist. This is a doctor who
L370@P12: specialises in arrhythmias.
L371@P12: Most people need only a local anaesthetic and
L372@P12: sedation before having this test. The test can take
L373@P12: about two to three hours.
L374@P12: The electrophysiologist will insert some special
L375@P12: catheters (long, thin tubes) into a large vein,
L376@P12: usually in the groin. The catheters are then gently
L377@P12: moved up through the veins and into your heart.
L378@P12: A small electrode at the tip of each catheter tries to
L379@P12: detect where any unwanted electrical impulses are
L380@P12: coming from.
